links.passage: Yaghi, Arslan and Naoum (2013) investigated the impacts of furrow and drip irrigation methods on tomato yields and water use efficiency under semi‐arid conditions. links.passage: In a tomato irrigation study by Mukherjee et al. (2023), drip irrigation reduced the total amount of water applied by about 21.2%. They argued that using a drip system to precisely apply irrigation at a soil matric potential of −10 kPa would cut the total water used and increase tomato yield and water productivity.

links.passage: El Marazky (2018) evaluated several irrigation scheduling approaches, including ET controllers, soil moisture sensors, and manual irrigation for tomato cultivation in Saudi Arabia. Their results showed that scheduling irrigation based on an ET controller conserved water by up to 26% compared to manual methods and 7% compared to the soil moisture system. The ET controller treatment also resulted in the highest yields, WUE, and fruit quality.
reference_entries: El Marazky, M. S. A. 2018. “Effects of Scheduling Techniques of Water Application for Drip Irrigation System on Tomato Yield in Arid Region. Egypt.” Journal of Agriculture Research 96, no. 1: 237–251.
